headings.title: Introduction to Food Nutrients
headings.content: Food nutrients are chemical substances obtained from food that are essential for growth, maintenance, repair, and overall health. For nursing students in Nigeria, understanding nutrition is critical because proper dietary intake directly influences patient recovery, immune function, and the prevention of chronic illnesses such as malnutrition, which remains a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa. Nutrients are broadly classified based on the quantity required by the body and their specific physiological functions. They include macronutrients, which are needed in large amounts to supply energy and build tissues, and micronutrients, which are required in trace amounts to regulate metabolic processes. Furthermore, water and dietary fiber play indispensable roles in maintaining homeostasis and supporting gastrointestinal health. As future nurses, you will assess patients' nutritional statuses, educate communities on balanced diets utilizing locally available foods, and collaborate with multidisciplinary healthcare teams to design individualized nutritional care plans. Recognizing the foundation of food nutrients allows clinicians to address both undernutrition and overnutrition effectively across diverse healthcare settings, ranging from rural primary health clinics to tertiary teaching hospitals. Ultimately, integrating nutritional science into nursing care promotes holistic healing and empowers patients to make informed dietary choices that sustain long-term well-being and prevent diet-related diseases.

headings.title: Macronutrients: Carbohydrates, Proteins, and Fats
headings.content: Macronutrients consist of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, and they form the bulk of the human diet, providing the energy and structural components necessary for survival. Carbohydrates are the primary and most rapid source of energy for the body, broken down into glucose to fuel cellular activities, especially in the brain and nervous system. In the Nigerian context, staple carbohydrate sources include cassava, yam, maize, millet, and rice. Proteins are complex organic molecules made up of amino acids, which are vital for tissue growth, cellular repair, immune defense, and enzyme synthesis. While animal sources like meat, fish, and eggs provide high biological value proteins, plant sources such as beans, cowpeas, and bambara nuts offer essential complementary proteins. Fats, also known as lipids, are concentrated sources of energy that provide protection for vital organs, facilitate the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins, and support cell membrane integrity. Nurses must educate patients on balancing these three macronutrients while choosing healthy unsaturated fats over trans fats and unrefined complex carbohydrates over simple sugars to prevent lifestyle diseases such as obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disorders. Understanding the specific roles and dietary sources of macronutrients enables nurses to provide culturally appropriate nutritional counseling to patients and their families.

headings.title: Micronutrients: Vitamins and Minerals
headings.content: Micronutrients comprise vitamins and minerals, which, although required in much smaller quantities than macronutrients, are absolutely critical for regulating physiological processes, maintaining immune competence, and supporting growth. Vitamins are organic compounds divided into water-soluble (such as Vitamin C and the B-complex group) and fat-soluble (such as Vitamins A, D, E, and K). Water-soluble vitamins need regular daily replenishment because excess amounts are excreted in urine, whereas fat-soluble vitamins can be stored in the liver and fatty tissues. Minerals are inorganic elements classified into major minerals (like calcium, potassium, and sodium) and trace minerals (like iron, zinc, and iodine). In Nigeria, micronutrient deficiencies—often referred to as hidden hunger—pose severe health threats, including iron-deficiency anemia, vitamin A deficiency leading to childhood blindness, and iodine deficiency causing goiter. Nurses play a frontline role in screening for these deficiencies, administering supplements, and promoting the consumption of locally available fruits, dark green leafy vegetables, and fortified foods. Educating mothers and caregivers on micronutrient-rich diets is a key nursing intervention to reduce maternal and child morbidity and mortality rates across healthcare facilities and community outreaches.

headings.title: The Vital Role of Water in Human Nutrition
headings.content: Water is often considered the most critical nutrient for human survival, constituting approximately 60% of an adult's total body weight. It serves as the fundamental medium for all cellular metabolic reactions, acts as a solvent for transporting nutrients and waste products, regulates body temperature through perspiration, and cushions vital organs and joints. In clinical nursing practice, monitoring fluid balance is a daily priority, especially for patients experiencing vomiting, diarrhea, burns, or fever, all of which put them at high risk for dehydration. In Nigeria, acute gastroenteritis and dehydration in children remain major contributors to hospital admissions, making oral rehydration therapy (ORT) education a vital competency for nurses. Patients must be taught the importance of drinking adequate clean water daily, accounting for environmental factors such as the tropical climate and high ambient temperatures which increase fluid loss through sweat. Nurses must also assess signs of hydration status, including skin turgor, mucous membrane moisture, urine output, and cognitive alertness. Failure to maintain proper hydration can lead to electrolyte imbalances, hypovolemic shock, acute kidney injury, and impaired drug metabolism. Therefore, incorporating fluid management into patient education and direct care is an indispensable pillar of nursing excellence.

headings.title: Dietary Fiber and Its Digestive Functions
headings.content: Dietary fiber, consisting of plant-based carbohydrates that cannot be fully digested by human gastrointestinal enzymes, plays a vital role in maintaining digestive health and metabolic function. Fiber is categorized into two main types: soluble fiber, which dissolves in water to form a gel-like substance that helps lower blood cholesterol and regulate blood glucose levels, and insoluble fiber, which adds bulk to stool and accelerates intestinal transit time to prevent constipation. Good Nigerian sources of dietary fiber include whole grains, beans, lentils, vegetables, and unrefined tubers. For hospitalized patients, especially those on prolonged bed rest or receiving opioid analgesics, constipation is a frequent and distressing complication; increasing dietary fiber intake combined with adequate hydration is a natural and effective preventative measure. Furthermore, fiber fermentation in the colon produces short-chain fatty acids that nourish colonocytes, support a healthy gut microbiome, and enhance immune defense. Nurses must guide patients to gradually increase fiber intake to avoid abdominal bloating and cramping. Incorporating fiber-rich local foods into meal plans also helps manage chronic conditions like diverticular disease, hemorrhoids, and type 2 diabetes, demonstrating the profound clinical value of this non-nutrient component in holistic nursing care.

headings.title: Digestion, Absorption, and Metabolism of Nutrients
headings.content: The journey of food nutrients involves three sequential and complex physiological processes: digestion, absorption, and metabolism. Digestion begins in the oral cavity through mechanical chewing and enzymatic action of saliva, continues in the stomach via gastric acids and pepsin, and reaches its peak in the small intestine where pancreatic enzymes and bile break down macronutrients into their simplest absorbable forms (monosaccharides, amino acids, fatty acids, and glycerol). Absorption primarily occurs across the microvilli of the small intestinal mucosa, where nutrients pass into the bloodstream or lymphatic system for systemic distribution. Water-soluble nutrients travel via the portal vein directly to the liver for processing, while fat-soluble nutrients are packaged into chylomicrons and transported through the lymphatic system. Once delivered to body cells, metabolism takes over. Metabolism encompasses anabolism, the constructive phase where simple molecules are built up into complex tissue structures, and catabolism, the destructive phase where molecules are broken down to release stored chemical energy. Nurses must understand these pathways to recognize how disease states—such as celiac disease, short bowel syndrome, liver cirrhosis, or pancreatic insufficiency—impair nutrient utilization. Assessing digestive symptoms, tracking bowel elimination, and collaborating with dietitians to provide appropriate enteral or parenteral nutrition are core competencies for nursing students.

headings.title: Nutritional Assessment and Dietary Guidelines in Nursing Practice
headings.content: Nutritional assessment is a systematic nursing process used to evaluate a patient's nutritional status, identify deficiencies or excesses, and guide clinical interventions. The assessment framework utilizes the ABCDE approach: Anthropometric measurements (height, weight, body mass index, mid-upper arm circumference), Biochemical data (serum albumin, hemoglobin levels, electrolyte panels), Clinical signs (appearance of skin, hair, nails, and oral cavity indicative of nutrient deficiencies), Dietary history (food frequency questionnaires, 24-hour dietary recalls), and Economic/environmental factors (access to food, cultural practices, socioeconomic status). In Nigeria, anthropometric tools like the MUAC tape are invaluable in community health nursing for rapid screening of malnutrition in infants and pregnant women. Based on assessment findings, nurses utilize national and international dietary guidelines to educate patients and formulate nursing diagnoses such as 'Imbalanced Nutrition: Less Than Body Requirements' or 'Risk for Unstable Blood Glucose.' Furthermore, nurses coordinate care with clinical dietitians, pharmacists, and medical officers to ensure patients receive adequate nutritional support, whether through modified hospital diets, therapeutic feeding formulas, or tube feedings. Effective nutritional assessment empowers nurses to advocate for vulnerable populations, monitor therapeutic outcomes, and foster sustainable health education within diverse Nigerian healthcare environments.
